notes:
Coordinate axes and octants

  • Space is divided by the three coordinate planes ($xy,yz,zx$) into 8 octants. All three planes meet at the origin $(0,0,0)$.
  • In the first octant all of $x,y,z$ are positive.

Distance formula

  • Distance between $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2,z_2)$: $d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2+(z_2-z_1)^2}$.
  • Distance from origin to $(x,y,z)$: $\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}$.

Section formula

  • Point dividing $AB$ internally in ratio $m:n$: $\left(\dfrac{mx_2+nx_1}{m+n},\dfrac{my_2+ny_1}{m+n},\dfrac{mz_2+nz_1}{m+n}\right)$.
  • Midpoint: average of corresponding coordinates. A negative ratio (e.g. $-2:3$) means external division.

Direction cosines (dc's) and direction ratios (dr's)

  • If a line makes angles $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ with the $x,y,z$ axes, its dc's are $l=\cos\alpha, m=\cos\beta, n=\cos\gamma$, and always $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$.
  • Any numbers $a,b,c$ proportional to $l,m,n$ are direction ratios; dc's are recovered by $l=\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$ (similarly for $m,n$).
  • Direction ratios of the line joining $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ are $(x_2-x_1, y_2-y_1, z_2-z_1)$.
  • A line making equal angles with all three axes has $l=m=n=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$.

Angle between two lines

  • Using dr's $(a_1,b_1,c_1)$ and $(a_2,b_2,c_2)$: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2}{\sqrt{a_1^2+b_1^2+c_1^2}\sqrt{a_2^2+b_2^2+c_2^2}}$.
  • Parallel lines: dr's proportional. Perpendicular lines: $a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2=0$.

Exam tip

KCET usually asks 1-2 questions from this introductory chapter — typically the distance formula, section formula (including external division), or checking whether two lines (given by direction ratios) are parallel/perpendicular. Do not confuse direction ratios (any proportional triple) with direction cosines (must satisfy $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$).

questions.q: The distance between the points $(1,2,3)$ and $(4,6,3)$ is
questions.trick: $d=\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2+(\Delta z)^2}$ — just extend Pythagoras to 3D.

questions.q: The distance of the point $(2,-3,6)$ from the origin is
questions.trick: Distance from origin $=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}$.

questions.q: The midpoint of the segment joining $(2,-3,4)$ and $(4,1,-2)$ is
questions.trick: Midpoint = average of each coordinate pair.

questions.q: The point dividing the segment joining $(1,-2,3)$ and $(3,4,-5)$ internally in the ratio $2:3$ is
questions.trick: Section formula: $\dfrac{mx_2+nx_1}{m+n}$ for each coordinate.

questions.q: The direction cosines of a line making equal angles with all three coordinate axes are
questions.trick: Equal angles $\Rightarrow l=m=n=\pm1/\sqrt3$.

questions.q: The direction ratios of the line joining $(1,2,-3)$ and $(4,-2,1)$ are
questions.trick: Dr's of $PQ$ = coordinates of $Q$ minus coordinates of $P$.

questions.q: The direction cosines of a line whose direction ratios are $2,3,-6$ are
questions.trick: Divide each direction ratio by $\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}$ to get dc's.

questions.q: Lines with direction ratios $(2,-1,2)$ and $(1,2,0)$ are
questions.trick: Perpendicular check: $a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2=0$.

questions.q: Lines with direction ratios $(2,4,-6)$ and $(1,2,-3)$ are
questions.explanation: $(2,4,-6) = 2\times(1,2,-3)$, so the direction ratios are proportional — the lines are parallel.
questions.trick: Parallel check: one triple is a scalar multiple of the other.

questions.q: The $YZ$-plane divides the segment joining $(2,4,5)$ and $(3,5,-4)$ in the ratio
questions.explanation: On the $YZ$-plane, $x=0$. For ratio $k:1$, $x=\dfrac{3k+2}{k+1}=0 \Rightarrow k=-\dfrac23$, i.e. ratio $-2:3$ (external division).
questions.trick: Plane $x=0$ divides in ratio $-x_1:x_2$ (external if signs differ).

questions.q: The three coordinate planes intersect at
questions.explanation: The $xy$, $yz$ and $zx$ planes are all common to only one point: the origin $(0,0,0)$.
questions.trick: All three coordinate planes meet only at the origin.

questions.q: If the direction cosines of a line are $k,k,k$, then $k$ equals
questions.explanation: $k^2+k^2+k^2=1 \Rightarrow 3k^2=1 \Rightarrow k=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$ (negative dc's represent the opposite direction).
questions.trick: $3k^2=1\Rightarrow k=\pm1/\sqrt3$ — don't forget both signs.

questions.q: The distance of the point $(3,4,5)$ from the $x$-axis is
questions.trick: Distance from $x$-axis $=\sqrt{y^2+z^2}$ (drop the $x$).

questions.q: The point $(2,3,4)$ lies in the
questions.explanation: All three coordinates are positive, which corresponds to the first octant.
questions.trick: All coordinates positive $\Rightarrow$ first octant, always.

questions.q: The direction ratios of a line perpendicular to both lines with direction ratios $(1,-2,-2)$ and $(0,2,1)$ are
questions.trick: Perpendicular to both lines $\Rightarrow$ take their cross product.

questions.q: The distance between $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ is given by
questions.explanation: The 3D distance formula extends the 2D one by adding the squared difference of $z$-coordinates under the root.
questions.trick: 3D distance = 2D formula plus $(\Delta z)^2$ under the root.

questions.q: If $a,b,c$ are the direction ratios of a line, its direction cosine $l$ equals
questions.explanation: Direction cosines are the direction ratios divided by the magnitude $\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}$.
questions.trick: $l=\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$ — dr divided by magnitude.

questions.q: For $P(1,2,3)$ and $Q(4,6,15)$, the direction cosines of line $PQ$ are
questions.trick: Find dr's $=Q-P$, then divide each by their magnitude.

questions.q: The distance of the point $(3,-4,5)$ from the $y$-axis is
questions.trick: Distance from $y$-axis $=\sqrt{x^2+z^2}$ (drop the $y$).

questions.q: The centroid of the triangle with vertices $(1,2,3), (3,4,5), (5,6,1)$ is
questions.trick: Centroid = average of the three vertices' coordinates, componentwise.

questions.q: The point dividing the segment joining $(2,3,4)$ and $(5,6,7)$ externally in the ratio $2:1$ is
questions.trick: External division: same formula but with a minus sign, $\dfrac{mx_2-nx_1}{m-n}$.

questions.q: The $XZ$-plane divides the segment joining $(1,2,3)$ and $(4,-5,6)$ in the ratio
questions.explanation: On the $XZ$-plane, $y=0$. For ratio $m:n$ from the first to second point, $\dfrac{m(-5)+n(2)}{m+n}=0 \Rightarrow m/n=2/5$, i.e. ratio $2:5$.
questions.trick: Plane $y=0$: set the $y$-section-formula expression to zero, solve $m:n$.

questions.q: The direction ratios of the $x$-axis are
questions.explanation: The $x$-axis points purely in the $x$-direction, so its direction ratios are $(1,0,0)$.
questions.trick: $x$-axis direction ratios are simply $(1,0,0)$.

questions.q: A line makes angles $90^\circ, 60^\circ, 30^\circ$ with the $x, y, z$ axes respectively. Its direction cosines are
questions.trick: $l=\cos\alpha,\ m=\cos\beta,\ n=\cos\gamma$ — plug angles in directly.

questions.q: A line has direction cosines $l=\dfrac13, m=\dfrac23$. Its positive direction cosine $n$ is
questions.trick: Use $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$ to solve for the missing dc.

questions.explanation: Direction ratios of both $(1,2,3)$-$(4,5,6)$ and $(4,5,6)$-$(7,8,9)$ are $(3,3,3)$, so the three points lie on the same line.
questions.trick: Same direction ratios between consecutive pairs $\Rightarrow$ collinear.

questions.q: The distance of the point $(1,2,2)$ from the origin is
questions.trick: Distance from origin $=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}$.

questions.q: The distance between the points $(0,3,-2)$ and $(0,-1,1)$ is
questions.trick: $d=\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2+(\Delta z)^2}$; here $\Delta x=0$ drops out.

questions.q: The direction cosines of a line with direction ratios $2,-2,1$ are
questions.trick: Dc's = dr's divided by $\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}$.

questions.q: A line has direction ratios $2,5,-4$. Taking $l,m,n$ as its direction cosines (positive magnitude), $l+m+n$ equals
questions.trick: Find magnitude first, then sum the dc's over that one magnitude.

questions.q: The distance of the point $(6,8,0)$ from the $z$-axis is
questions.trick: Distance from $z$-axis $=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ (drop the $z$).

questions.q: A point $P$ on the line joining $(3,-2,1)$ and $(1,4,-3)$ has $x$-coordinate 2. $P$ divides the segment in the ratio
questions.explanation: For ratio $m:n$ from the first point, $\dfrac{m(1)+n(3)}{m+n}=2 \Rightarrow m+3n=2m+2n \Rightarrow m=n$, i.e. ratio $1:1$ (the midpoint).
questions.trick: Set the section-formula $x$-expression equal to the known $x$-coordinate, solve $m:n$.

questions.q: Which of the following can be the direction cosines of a line?
questions.explanation: Direction cosines must satisfy $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$. Only $\left(-\dfrac1{\sqrt3},-\dfrac1{\sqrt3},-\dfrac1{\sqrt3}\right)$ gives $3\times\dfrac13=1$; the others do not.
questions.trick: Check $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$ for each option — only one satisfies it.

questions.q: The angle between lines with direction ratios $(1,2,-2)$ and $(2,2,1)$ has cosine equal to
questions.trick: $\cos\theta=\dfrac{a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2}{|\vec{d_1}||\vec{d_2}|}$ — dot product over magnitudes.

questions.q: The distance of the point $(x,y,z)$ from the origin is
questions.explanation: The distance formula from the origin is the square root of the sum of the squares of the coordinates.
questions.trick: Distance from origin: just $\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}$, no shortcuts needed.

questions.q: The direction ratios of the line joining $(2,3,-1)$ and $(2,3,4)$ are proportional to
questions.explanation: Dr's $=(2-2,3-3,4-(-1))=(0,0,5)$, proportional to $(0,0,1)$ — the line is parallel to the $z$-axis.
questions.trick: Only $z$ changes between the points $\Rightarrow$ line is parallel to $z$-axis.

questions.q: Two lines have direction ratios proportional to $(1,-2,1)$ and $(2,3,4)$. The lines are
questions.trick: Dot product of dr's $=0$ means perpendicular.

questions.q: The point on the $z$-axis equidistant from $(1,2,3)$ and $(3,2,1)$ is
questions.explanation: Let the point be $(0,0,z)$. Setting the squared distances equal: $5+(z-3)^2=13+(z-1)^2 \Rightarrow -4z=0 \Rightarrow z=0$, giving $(0,0,0)$.
questions.trick: Point on $z$-axis is $(0,0,z)$; equate squared distances to the two points.

questions.q: The three coordinate planes divide space into how many octants?
questions.explanation: The $xy$, $yz$ and $zx$ planes together divide space into 8 octants.
questions.trick: Three coordinate planes always split space into 8 octants.

questions.q: The direction cosines of the $z$-axis are
questions.explanation: The $z$-axis points purely in the $z$-direction, so its direction cosines are $(0,0,1)$.
questions.trick: $z$-axis direction cosines are simply $(0,0,1)$.
